statement: For a smooth flow of an inviscid, barotropic fluid with conservative body forces and [vorticity](c:vorticity) $\omega = \nabla \times u$: (1) a vortex tube has the same strength along its length; (2) [vortex lines](c:vortex-line) move with the fluid; (3) the strength of a vortex tube does not change in time. The strength of a tube is the [circulation](c:circulation) around it.

hypotheses.text: The velocity field $u$ is smooth and obeys the [Euler equations](c:euler-equations), so the flow is inviscid.
The density is a function of the pressure alone.
The body force per unit mass is $-\nabla\chi$ for a smooth potential $\chi$.

conclusion: The vorticity flux is equal across all cross-sections of a vortex tube, vortex lines stay vortex lines, and the strength of a carried vortex tube is constant in time.

proofs.name: Divergence theorem and Kelvin's theorem
proofs.slogan: Part (1) follows from the zero divergence of the vorticity; parts (2) and (3) follow from Kelvin's circulation theorem.
proofs.scope: The vorticity must be nonzero for a vortex line to exist, so part (2) excludes zeros of $\omega$. The fluid need not be incompressible; compressibility enters only through the barotropic law inside Kelvin's theorem.

roles.why: Smoothness of $u$ gives $\nabla\cdot\omega=0$, and the Euler equations are the momentum balance behind Kelvin's theorem.
A density that depends on the pressure alone makes the acceleration a gradient inside Kelvin's theorem.
A potential body force adds a gradient to the acceleration, so circulation stays constant.

steps.slogan: Equate the vorticity fluxes through two cross-sections of a vortex tube.
steps.detail: The field $\omega=\nabla\times u$ has zero [divergence](c:divergence) for smooth $u$. On the side wall of the tube $\omega$ is tangent, so the divergence theorem on the tube segment between two cross-sections gives equal fluxes through them. By Stokes' theorem the flux through a cross-section is the [circulation](c:circulation) around its edge, which is the strength of the tube.

steps.slogan: Conserve the circulation around every closed loop that moves with the fluid.
steps.detail: The three hypotheses are those of Kelvin's circulation theorem. So $\oint_{C(t)}u\cdot dl$ is constant in time for every closed curve $C(t)$ made of the same fluid particles.

steps.slogan: Show that a surface made of vortex lines stays a surface of vortex lines.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be a surface made of vortex lines at time $t_0$, so $\omega\cdot n=0$ on $S$. By Stokes' theorem every small closed loop in $S$ has zero circulation. The [flow](c:flow-of-a-vector-field) carries $S$ to a surface $S(t)$ and its loops to loops on $S(t)$, and by step 2 their circulation stays zero. Hence $\omega\cdot n=0$ on $S(t)$.

steps.slogan: Write a vortex line as the meeting of two surfaces of vortex lines.
steps.detail: Near a point with $\omega\ne0$, a vortex line is the transversal intersection of two surfaces made of vortex lines, for example level surfaces of two independent first integrals of $\omega$. By step 3 the moved surfaces keep this property and stay transversal, so the moved line is tangent to $\omega$. This proves part (2).

steps.slogan: Show that the strength of a vortex tube stays constant in time.
steps.detail: By step 4 the moved tube is again a vortex tube. A loop around the tube is a closed material curve, so its circulation, which is the strength, is constant by step 2. This proves part (3).

steps.slogan: Combine the three parts into the three theorems of Helmholtz.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives part (1) on the strength along a tube. Step 4 gives part (2) on vortex lines. Step 5 gives part (3) on the strength in time.

concepts.c:vorticity: Vorticity is the field whose flux defines the strength of a tube.
concepts.c:vortex-line: Vortex lines are the curves whose motion part (2) describes.
concepts.c:circulation: Circulation around a loop is conserved and equals the vorticity flux.
concepts.c:euler-equations: The Euler equations are the inviscid momentum balance of the flow.
concepts.c:divergence: Zero divergence of vorticity makes the flux through a tube constant.
concepts.c:flow-of-a-vector-field: The flow carries surfaces and loops of fluid forward in time.

source.note: The classical derivation of Helmholtz's theorems from Kelvin's circulation theorem, as in Batchelor, An Introduction to Fluid Dynamics (Cambridge University Press, 1967), in the treatment of vorticity in an inviscid fluid.

new_concepts.name: vorticity
new_concepts.reminder: Vorticity is the curl of the velocity field of a fluid; it measures the local rotation of the flow.
new_concepts.definition: The vorticity of a flow with velocity field $u$ is the vector field $\omega=\nabla\times u$.

new_concepts.name: vortex line
new_concepts.reminder: A vortex line is a curve that is everywhere tangent to the vorticity field.
new_concepts.definition: A vortex line is an integral curve of the vorticity field; the vortex lines through a small closed curve form a vortex tube.

statement: Every [finitely generated](c:finitely-generated-group) [recursively presented group](c:recursively-presented-group) embeds as a subgroup in some [finitely presented group](c:finitely-presented-group).

hypotheses.text: The group $R$ is [finitely generated](c:finitely-generated-group).
The group $R$ has a presentation on its finitely many generators with a [recursively enumerable](c:recursively-enumerable-set) set of defining relators.

conclusion: There is a finitely presented group $G$ and an injective homomorphism $R\to G$.

proofs.name: Benign subgroups of free groups
proofs.slogan: Show that every recursively enumerable normal subgroup of a finitely generated free group is benign, then embed the quotient in a finitely presented group.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of Higman's proof. The converse, that a finitely presented group is recursively presented, is immediate and is not part of the statement.

roles.why: A finite generating set gives a finitely generated [free group](c:free-group) $F$ that maps onto $R$.
The recursively enumerable relators make the kernel a recursively enumerable subset of $F$.

steps.slogan: Write $R$ as the quotient of a free group by an enumerable normal subgroup.
steps.detail: Let $F$ be free on the finite generating set of $R$ and let $N$ be the normal closure of the recursively enumerable relators. Then $R\cong F/N$, and $N$ is a [recursively enumerable](c:recursively-enumerable-set) subset of $F$.

steps.slogan: Define benign subgroups of a finitely generated free group.
steps.detail: A subgroup $H\le F$ is benign if $F$ embeds in a finitely presented group $G$ in which some finitely generated subgroup $K$ satisfies $K\cap F=H$. Higman builds the closure properties of benign subgroups with [amalgamated products](c:amalgamated-product) and [HNN extensions](c:hnn-extension).

steps.slogan: Close the benign subgroups under Higman's operations on subsets.
steps.detail: Higman shows that a short list of operations on subsets preserves benignness. The same operations, applied to two initial subsets, produce exactly the recursively enumerable subsets.

steps.slogan: Prove that every recursively enumerable subgroup of $F$ is benign.
steps.detail: Higman's characterization of recursively enumerable sets by operations, with step 3, shows that each recursively enumerable subgroup of $F$ is benign. In particular the normal subgroup $N$ is benign in $F$.

steps.slogan: Embed $F/N$ in a finitely presented group built from the benign witness.
steps.detail: Take a finitely presented $G\supseteq F$ and a finitely generated $K\le G$ with $K\cap F=N$. Amalgamated products and HNN extensions of $G$ along $K$ give a [finitely presented group](c:finitely-presented-group) that contains $F/N\cong R$.

concepts.c:finitely-generated-group: Finite generation gives a free group of finite rank mapping onto $R$.
concepts.c:recursively-presented-group: Recursive presentation makes the relation subgroup recursively enumerable.
concepts.c:finitely-presented-group: A finitely presented group is the target of the embedding.
concepts.c:recursively-enumerable-set: Enumerability of relators matches the operations that generate benign subgroups.
concepts.c:free-group: The free group is the ambient group where benign subgroups live.
concepts.c:amalgamated-product: Amalgamated products build the finitely presented groups that witness benignness.
concepts.c:hnn-extension: HNN extensions build the finitely presented groups that witness benignness.

source.ref: G. Higman, Subgroups of finitely presented groups, Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, Series A 262 (1961), 455-475
source.note: The steps follow Higman's paper: benign subgroups, closure under his operations on subsets, the theorem that recursively enumerable subgroups of free groups are benign, and the embedding.

statement: If two sides of a [triangle](c:triangle) have equal length, then the [angles](c:angle) opposite them are equal: when $|p_1p_2|=|p_1p_3|$, then $\angle p_1p_2p_3=\angle p_1p_3p_2$.

hypotheses.text: The sides $p_1p_2$ and $p_1p_3$ of the triangle have equal length, $\operatorname{dist}(p_1,p_2)=\operatorname{dist}(p_1,p_3)$.

conclusion: The angles at $p_2$ and at $p_3$ are equal.

formal.difference: The declaration works in an affine space over any real inner product space and does not require three distinct points. For coincident points both angles are $\pi/2$ by the convention of the arccos formula.

proofs.name: Vector form with cosines
proofs.slogan: Write the base angles as angles between vectors and compare their cosines.
proofs.scope: Any dimension, and degenerate triples are allowed. If $x=0$ then $y=0$ and both angles are $\pi/2$ by the convention that a quotient by a zero norm is zero.

roles.why: The equal norms $\|x\|=\|y\|$ make the two cosines equal.

steps.slogan: Write both base angles as angles between vectors.
steps.detail: Put $x=p_1-p_2$ and $y=p_1-p_3$, so $p_3-p_2=x-y$. Then $\angle p_1p_2p_3=\angle(x,x-y)$ and $\angle p_1p_3p_2=\angle(y,y-x)$, and the hypothesis says $\|x\|=\|y\|$.

steps.slogan: Reduce equality of the two angles to equality of their cosines.
steps.detail: The [angle](c:angle) between two vectors is $\arccos$ of $\langle u,v\rangle/(\|u\|\|v\|)$, so it lies in $[0,\pi]$. The cosine is injective on $[0,\pi]$, so it is enough to show that the two cosines are equal.

steps.slogan: Expand both inner products and use the equal norms.
steps.detail: The real inner product is symmetric, so $\langle x,x-y\rangle=\|x\|^2-\langle x,y\rangle$ and $\langle y,y-x\rangle=\|y\|^2-\langle x,y\rangle$. These agree because $\|x\|=\|y\|$. Also $\|x-y\|=\|y-x\|$, so the two quotients are equal.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the two base angles are equal.
steps.detail: The two cosines are equal and both angles lie in $[0,\pi]$. Hence $\angle p_1p_2p_3=\angle p_1p_3p_2$.

concepts.c:triangle: The theorem concerns the base angles of a triangle with two equal sides.
concepts.c:angle: Angles are defined through the arccos of a normalized inner product.

source.note: mathlib reduces to the vector form InnerProductGeometry.angle_sub_eq_angle_sub_rev_of_norm_eq, proved with Real.injOn_cos and the formula Real.cos_angle.

proofs.name: Congruence of the triangle with its relabeling
proofs.slogan: Read the triangle twice, as $p_1p_2p_3$ and as $p_1p_3p_2$, and use side-angle-side congruence.
proofs.scope: A nondegenerate triangle, with $p_1,p_2,p_3$ distinct and not collinear. The side-angle-side rule is taken as known.

roles.why: Equal sides at $p_1$ make the two readings match side by side.

steps.slogan: Compare the triangle $p_1p_2p_3$ with the same triangle read as $p_1p_3p_2$.
steps.detail: Both readings have the same three points. At $p_1$ the sides are $p_1p_2,p_1p_3$ in the first reading and $p_1p_3,p_1p_2$ in the second.

steps.slogan: Show that the two readings are congruent by side-angle-side.
steps.detail: The sides at $p_1$ are equal in pairs, since $|p_1p_2|=|p_1p_3|$ by hypothesis. The angle between them is $\angle p_2p_1p_3$ in both readings. So the triangles are [congruent](c:congruence), with $p_2$ matched to $p_3$.

steps.slogan: Read the equal base angles from the congruence.
steps.detail: Corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal. The angle at $p_2$ in the first reading corresponds to the angle at $p_3$ in the second, so $\angle p_1p_2p_3=\angle p_1p_3p_2$.

concepts.c:congruence: Congruence of the two readings transfers angles from one to the other.
concepts.c:triangle: The theorem concerns the base angles of a triangle with two equal sides.
concepts.c:angle: The conclusion equates two angles of the triangle.

source.note: Pappus of Alexandria's proof of Euclid, Elements I.5: the triangle is compared with its own relabeling by side-angle-side.

statement: For a connected [semisimple Lie group](c:semisimple-lie-group) $G$ with [Cartan decomposition](c:cartan-decomposition) $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak k\oplus\mathfrak p$, a maximal abelian $\mathfrak a\subseteq\mathfrak p$ and $\mathfrak n$ the sum of the positive restricted root spaces, the product map $K\times A\times N\to G$, $(k,a,n)\mapsto kan$, is an analytic [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph). Here $K,A,N$ are the analytic subgroups of $\mathfrak k,\mathfrak a,\mathfrak n$.

hypotheses.text: The Lie group $G$ is connected.
The Lie group $G$ is [semisimple](c:semisimple-lie-group): its [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$ is semisimple.
A [Cartan decomposition](c:cartan-decomposition) $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak k\oplus\mathfrak p$ is fixed, and $\mathfrak a\subseteq\mathfrak p$ is a maximal abelian subspace.
The subalgebra $\mathfrak n$ is the sum of the restricted root spaces of a chosen positive system for the roots of $\mathfrak a$.

conclusion: Every $g\in G$ is $g=kan$ for unique $k\in K$, $a\in A$, $n\in N$, and $g$ depends analytically on $(k,a,n)$ with analytic inverse.

proofs.name: Structure of AN and an open-closed argument
proofs.slogan: Split the Lie algebra, show that the product map is a bijective local diffeomorphism, and conclude with the inverse function theorem.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of the proof in Knapp's book; the steps rest on the structure theory of semisimple Lie algebras developed there. The subgroup $K$ need not be compact when the center of $G$ is infinite.

roles.why: Connectedness lets an open and closed image fill the whole group.
Semisimplicity gives the restricted root decomposition and makes central elements of $AN$ trivial.
The Cartan decomposition and the involution $\theta$ separate $\mathfrak k$ from $\mathfrak a\oplus\mathfrak n$.
The positive roots define $\mathfrak n$ and make $\mathfrak a\oplus\mathfrak n$ solvable.

steps.slogan: Split the Lie algebra as a vector space sum of $\mathfrak k$, $\mathfrak a$ and $\mathfrak n$.
steps.detail: The restricted root decomposition of the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$ under $\mathfrak a$, with the Cartan involution $\theta$, gives $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak k\oplus\mathfrak a\oplus\mathfrak n$. This is the Iwasawa decomposition of $\mathfrak g$.

steps.slogan: Show that $AN$ is a simply connected solvable group parametrized by its Lie algebra.
steps.detail: The algebra $\mathfrak a\oplus\mathfrak n$ is solvable, $\mathfrak n$ is nilpotent, and $\mathfrak a$ acts on $\mathfrak n$ with real eigenvalues. So the exponential map is a diffeomorphism from $\mathfrak a\oplus\mathfrak n$ onto $AN$.

steps.slogan: Show that the product map has a bijective differential at every point.
steps.detail: At the identity the differential is the sum map $\mathfrak k\oplus\mathfrak a\oplus\mathfrak n\to\mathfrak g$, a bijection by step 1. The map $(k,b)\mapsto kb$ on $K\times AN$ commutes with left translation by $K$ and right translation by $AN$, so the differential is bijective everywhere. The inverse function theorem makes the map a [local diffeomorphism](c:local-diffeomorphism).

steps.slogan: Show that $K\cap AN$ is trivial, so the product map is injective.
steps.detail: The group $\mathrm{Ad}(K)$ preserves a positive definite form, so its eigenvalues have modulus one. The group $\mathrm{Ad}(AN)$ has positive real eigenvalues. An element $k=\exp Y$ of the intersection therefore has $\mathrm{Ad}(k)=1$, which forces $Y=0$ because $\mathfrak g$ is semisimple.

steps.slogan: Show that the product map is onto the connected group $G$.
steps.detail: The image $K\cdot AN$ is open by step 3. The cited proof shows that it is also closed in $G$. A nonempty open and closed subset of the connected group $G$ is $G$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the product map is an analytic diffeomorphism.
steps.detail: The map is a bijection by steps 4 and 5, and its differential is bijective everywhere by step 3. By the inverse function theorem its inverse is analytic, so it is an analytic [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph).

concepts.c:semisimple-lie-group: Semisimplicity supplies the root structure that the whole proof uses.
concepts.c:cartan-decomposition: The Cartan decomposition separates the compact part $\mathfrak k$ from $\mathfrak p$.
concepts.c:diffeomorph: The theorem states that the product map is a diffeomorphism.
concepts.c:lie-algebra: The proof starts from a splitting of the Lie algebra of $G$.
concepts.c:local-diffeomorphism: A bijective differential makes the product map a local diffeomorphism.

source.ref: A. W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, second edition, Birkhauser, 2002, Chapter VI, Theorem 6.46
source.note: Knapp proves the Iwasawa decomposition of g in Chapter VI and then the group-level diffeomorphism; the steps give the structure of that argument.

statement: The complement of a [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve) $C$ in the plane $\mathbb R^2$ has exactly two [connected components](c:connected-component), one bounded and one unbounded, and $C$ is the [boundary](c:boundary) of each of them.

hypotheses.text: The set $C\subset\mathbb R^2$ is a [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve): the image of a continuous injective map from the circle.

conclusion: The set $\mathbb R^2\setminus C$ has exactly two components, a bounded interior and an unbounded exterior, and each has boundary $C$; so every path from one to the other meets $C$.

proofs.name: Homology of complements in the sphere
proofs.slogan: Pass to the sphere, count the components of the complement with a Mayer-Vietoris sequence, and show that each has the whole curve as boundary.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of the homological proof in Hatcher; step 2 is the cited input and steps 1 and 5 are the passage between the plane and the sphere. The curve is the full circle, so it splits into two arcs.

roles.why: The embedding gives two arcs whose union is $C$ and whose intersection is two points.

steps.slogan: Pass from the plane to the sphere by adding a point at infinity.
steps.detail: View $\mathbb R^2\subset S^2=\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$. The curve $C$ is a compact subset of $S^2$ that misses $\infty$, so it is enough to study the components of $S^2\setminus C$.

steps.slogan: Show that the complement of an arc in the sphere has trivial reduced homology.
steps.detail: For every embedded arc $A\subset S^2$ the reduced [homology](c:homology) groups of $S^2\setminus A$ are all zero. Hatcher proves this by induction on the dimension of an embedded disk, with Mayer-Vietoris sequences and a bisection argument.

steps.slogan: Count the components of $S^2\setminus C$ with a Mayer-Vietoris sequence.
steps.detail: Write $C=A\cup B$ with arcs $A,B$ meeting in two points $p,q$. Mayer-Vietoris for $S^2\setminus\{p,q\}=(S^2\setminus A)\cup(S^2\setminus B)$ and step 2 give $\tilde H_0(S^2\setminus C)\cong\tilde H_1(S^2\setminus\{p,q\})\cong\mathbb Z$. So $S^2\setminus C$ has exactly two path components, which are its [connected components](c:connected-component).

steps.slogan: Show that each component of $S^2\setminus C$ has all of $C$ as boundary.
steps.detail: Suppose a point $x\in C$ misses the closure of a component $U$. Remove a small open arc of $C$ around $x$ to get an arc $D$. By step 2 the set $S^2\setminus D$ is connected, but $U$ is open and closed in it and the other component is not in $U$, which is impossible.

steps.slogan: Return to the plane and find the bounded and the unbounded component.
steps.detail: The point $\infty$ lies in one component $U$. Then $U\setminus\{\infty\}$ is connected and unbounded. The other component $V$ has compact closure $V\cup C$ in $\mathbb R^2$, so it is bounded. These two sets are the components of $\mathbb R^2\setminus C$, and each has [boundary](c:boundary) $C$.

concepts.c:simple-closed-curve: The hypothesis is that $C$ is a simple closed curve.
concepts.c:connected-component: The theorem counts the connected components of the complement.
concepts.c:homology: Homology of the complement counts its components.
concepts.c:boundary: Both components must have the whole curve as boundary.

source.ref: A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Cambridge University Press, 2002, Section 2.B (Classical Applications): the Jordan-Brouwer separation theorem
source.note: Steps 2 to 4 follow Hatcher's argument for an embedded circle in the sphere; steps 1 and 5 pass between the plane and the sphere.

statement: Let $F\colon\Omega\to Y$ be a differentiable map between [Banach spaces](c:banach-space) whose derivative is [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function), and let the start point $x_0$ satisfy the Kantorovich bounds with $h\le\frac12$. Then [Newton's method](c:newton-s-method) from $x_0$ stays in the ball $\bar B(x_0,t_*)$ and converges to a root $x_*$ of $F$, with $\|x_*-x_k\|\le t_*-t_k$.

hypotheses.text: The spaces $X,Y$ are Banach spaces, $\Omega\subseteq X$ is open, and $F\colon\Omega\to Y$ is [Fréchet differentiable](c:frechet-derivative).
The derivative satisfies $\|F'(x)-F'(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in\Omega$.
At $x_0\in\Omega$ the derivative $F'(x_0)$ is invertible with $\|F'(x_0)^{-1}\|\le\beta$ and $\|F'(x_0)^{-1}F(x_0)\|\le\eta$.
The number $h=\beta L\eta$ is at most $\frac12$, and the closed ball $\bar B(x_0,t_*)$ with $t_*=(1-\sqrt{1-2h})/(\beta L)$ lies in $\Omega$.

conclusion: The Newton iterates $x_{k+1}=x_k-F'(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)$ are defined, lie in $\bar B(x_0,t_*)$ and converge to a root $x_*$ of $F$, with $\|x_*-x_k\|\le t_*-t_k$ for the scalar Newton iterates $t_k$ of $\varphi(t)=\frac L2t^2-\frac t\beta+\frac\eta\beta$ from $t_0=0$. If $h<\frac12$ and $B(x_0,t_{**})\subseteq\Omega$, where $t_{**}=(1+\sqrt{1-2h})/(\beta L)$, then $x_*$ is the only root in $B(x_0,t_{**})$.

proofs.name: Majorant sequence
proofs.slogan: Dominate the Newton steps by those of a scalar quadratic, then pass to the limit in the Banach space.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for arbitrary Banach spaces. Uniqueness needs $h<\frac12$ and the ball of radius $t_{**}$ inside $\Omega$; for $h=\frac12$ the roots of $\varphi$ coincide and only the first part is claimed.

roles.why: Differentiability gives the remainder bound, and completeness of $X$ gives the limit of the iterates.
The Lipschitz bound controls the inverse of the derivative and the remainder of the linearization.
The constants $\beta$ and $\eta$ define the majorant $\varphi$ and the first step.
The condition $h\le\frac12$ gives real roots of $\varphi$, and the ball condition keeps the iterates inside $\Omega$.

steps.slogan: Define the majorant quadratic and show that its Newton iterates increase to $t_*$.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi(t)=\frac L2t^2-\frac t\beta+\frac\eta\beta$, a [quadratic](c:quadratic-function) with discriminant $(1-2h)/\beta^2\ge0$. It has roots $t_*\le t_{**}$, and $t_*\le1/(\beta L)$. [Newton's method](c:newton-s-method) for the convex decreasing function $\varphi$ on $[0,t_*)$ gives $0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_*$ with $t_k\to t_*$.

steps.slogan: Bound the inverse of the derivative at any point near the start.
steps.detail: Let $\|x-x_0\|\le t<t_*$ and $\Gamma_0=F'(x_0)^{-1}$. Then $\|I-\Gamma_0F'(x)\|\le\beta Lt<1$, so a Neumann series makes $F'(x)$ invertible with $\|F'(x)^{-1}\|\le\beta/(1-\beta Lt)=-1/\varphi'(t)$.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction that the iterates stay near the start and the steps shrink like the majorant.
steps.detail: For $k=0$, $\|x_1-x_0\|\le\eta=t_1-t_0$. If $\|x_j-x_{j-1}\|\le t_j-t_{j-1}$ for $j\le k$, then $\|x_k-x_0\|\le t_k$ and $F'(x_k)$ is invertible by step 2. The integral form of the remainder gives $\|F(x_k)\|\le\frac L2\|x_k-x_{k-1}\|^2\le\varphi(t_k)$, so $\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\le\varphi(t_k)/(-\varphi'(t_k))=t_{k+1}-t_k$.

steps.slogan: Show that the iterates form a Cauchy sequence that converges in the ball.
steps.detail: The series $\sum_k(t_{k+1}-t_k)$ converges to $t_*$, so $(x_k)$ is a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) in the complete space $X$. Its limit $x_*$ lies in the closed ball $\bar B(x_0,t_*)\subseteq\Omega$, and $\|x_*-x_k\|\le\sum_{j\ge k}(t_{j+1}-t_j)=t_*-t_k$.

steps.slogan: Show that the limit is a root of $F$.
steps.detail: The Newton step gives $F(x_k)=-F'(x_k)(x_{k+1}-x_k)$. The norms $\|F'(x_k)\|\le\|F'(x_0)\|+Lt_*$ are bounded and $\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0$, so $F(x_k)\to0$. As $F$ is continuous, $F(x_*)=0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the errors of another root by a quadratic recursion.
steps.detail: Let $F(y)=0$ with $\|y-x_0\|<t_{**}$ and $e_k=\|y-x_k\|$. Since $y-x_{k+1}=-F'(x_k)^{-1}[F(y)-F(x_k)-F'(x_k)(y-x_k)]$, step 2 gives $e_{k+1}\le c_ke_k^2$ with $c_k=\beta L/(2(1-\beta Lt_k))$. The majorant satisfies $t_{**}-t_{k+1}=c_k(t_{**}-t_k)^2$ exactly.

steps.slogan: Show that every root in the larger ball equals the limit.
steps.detail: The ratio $r_k=e_k/(t_{**}-t_k)$ satisfies $r_{k+1}\le r_k^2$ and $r_0=\|y-x_0\|/t_{**}<1$. So $r_k\to0$ and $e_k\le r_kt_{**}\to0$. Hence $x_k\to y$, so $y=x_*$ and $x_*$ is the only root in the ball.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness of $X$ lets the Cauchy sequence of iterates converge.
concepts.c:lipschitz-continuous-function: The Lipschitz derivative bounds the linearization error by a quadratic term.
concepts.c:newton-s-method: The theorem describes the convergence of Newton's method from the start point.
concepts.c:frechet-derivative: The derivative $F'$ defines the Newton step and the linearization.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: The summable step bounds make the iterates a Cauchy sequence.
concepts.c:quadratic-function: The scalar quadratic majorant has explicit roots and explicit Newton iterates.

source.note: The majorant-sequence proof of Kantorovich (1948) in the form of J. M. Ortega, The Newton-Kantorovich theorem, American Mathematical Monthly 75 (1968), 658-660; the error-ratio argument for uniqueness is added here.

statement: In a smooth flow of an inviscid, barotropic fluid with conservative body forces, the [circulation](c:circulation) $\Gamma(t)=\oint_{C(t)}u\cdot dl$ around a [closed curve](c:closed-curve) $C(t)$ that moves with the fluid is constant in time.

hypotheses.text: The smooth velocity field $u$ obeys the [Euler equations](c:euler-equations), $\rho\,Du/Dt=-\nabla p+\rho f$.
The density is a function of the pressure alone, $\rho=\rho(p)$.
The body force per unit mass is $f=-\nabla\chi$ for a smooth potential $\chi$.
The curve $C(t)$ is closed and always consists of the same fluid particles.

conclusion: The circulation is constant: $\Gamma(t)=\Gamma(0)$ for all times $t$ of the flow.

proofs.name: Differentiate along the flow
proofs.slogan: Differentiate the circulation along the flow and show that both terms are integrals of exact derivatives around a closed loop.
proofs.scope: The flow and the curve are smooth on the time interval considered. The fluid need not be incompressible.

roles.why: Smoothness allows the time derivative inside the integral, and the Euler equations give the acceleration.
A density that depends on pressure alone turns the pressure term into a gradient.
A potential body force adds a gradient to the acceleration.
The labeled particles define the integral, and closure of the curve makes boundary terms cancel.

steps.slogan: Label the particles of the curve and write the circulation as an integral.
steps.detail: Let $x(s,t)$, $s\in[0,1]$, be the position at time $t$ of the particle with label $s$, so $x(0,t)=x(1,t)$ and $\partial_tx=u(x,t)$. The [circulation](c:circulation) is $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(x(s,t),t)\cdot\partial_sx\,ds$, a [line integral](c:line-integral) along the moving curve.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the circulation integral in time along the flow.
steps.detail: The product rule and $\partial_s\partial_tx=\partial_s[u(x(s,t),t)]$ give $\Gamma'(t)=\int_0^1\frac{Du}{Dt}\cdot\partial_sx\,ds+\int_0^1u\cdot\partial_s[u(x(s,t),t)]\,ds$. Here $Du/Dt$ is the acceleration of a particle.

steps.slogan: Write the acceleration as a gradient using the barotropic law and the potential.
Integrate both exact terms around the closed loop to get zero.
steps.detail: In the second integral $u\cdot\partial_s[u]=\partial_s(\tfrac12|u|^2)$. In the first, $-\nabla(P+\chi)\cdot\partial_sx=-\partial_s[(P+\chi)(x(s,t),t)]$. Both integrands are $s$-derivatives of functions with equal values at $s=0$ and $s=1$, so both integrals vanish by the fundamental theorem of calculus.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the derivative of the circulation is zero.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 4 give $\Gamma'(t)=0$ for every time $t$ of the flow. Hence $\Gamma$ is constant, and $\Gamma(t)=\Gamma(0)$.

concepts.c:circulation: Circulation is the quantity whose constancy the theorem states.
concepts.c:closed-curve: Closure of the material curve makes the loop integrals vanish.
concepts.c:euler-equations: The Euler equations give the acceleration of each fluid particle.
concepts.c:line-integral: The circulation is a line integral along the moving curve.

source.note: The classical proof by differentiating the circulation along the flow, as in Batchelor, An Introduction to Fluid Dynamics (Cambridge University Press, 1967).

statement: No [sphere packing](c:sphere-packing) of three-dimensional space by congruent balls has density greater than $\pi/\sqrt{18}\approx0.7405$, the density of the face-centred cubic packing.

hypotheses.text: A packing of $\mathbb R^3$ by balls of equal radius with disjoint interiors.

conclusion: The density of the packing is at most $\pi/\sqrt{18}$, and the face-centred cubic [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) packing attains this value.

proofs.name: Hales's computer-assisted proof
proofs.slogan: Reduce the density bound to a score inequality for decomposition stars, then check it over all tame plane graphs by linear programming.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of Hales's proof; steps 3 and 4 rest on computer enumeration and computation. The bound holds for every packing, not only for lattice packings.

roles.why: The packing is the object whose density the local scores bound.

steps.slogan: Reduce the density bound to a local inequality around each ball.
steps.detail: Hales splits space into decomposition stars, one cluster of cells around each ball, as a hybrid of Voronoi cells and Delaunay simplices. The density of a [packing](c:sphere-packing) is controlled by a sum over the balls of a local quantity.

steps.slogan: Define a score so that the conjecture follows from a bound of $8\,\mathrm{pt}$ per star.
steps.detail: Hales and Ferguson define a score function on decomposition stars. The stars of the face-centred cubic and hexagonal close packings have score exactly $8\,\mathrm{pt}$, and a score of at most $8\,\mathrm{pt}$ for every star implies the density bound $\pi/\sqrt{18}$.

steps.slogan: Encode each star that could break the bound as a plane graph and list all possible graphs.
steps.detail: A counterexample to the bound gives a [planar graph](c:planar-graph) with strong restrictions on its faces and vertices, called a tame graph. A computer enumeration lists all tame graphs; there are a few thousand.

steps.slogan: Bound the score of every tame graph with linear programs.
steps.detail: For each tame graph Hales bounds the score by [linear programming](c:linear-programming), with coefficients from nonlinear inequalities that a computer proves by interval arithmetic. Every case except the stars of the two close packings scores below $8\,\mathrm{pt}$, and a few exceptional graphs need separate arguments.

steps.slogan: Conclude that every packing has density at most $\pi/\sqrt{18}$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 4 give a score of at most $8\,\mathrm{pt}$ for every star, so by step 2 no packing is denser than $\pi/\sqrt{18}$. The face-centred cubic packing has this density, so the bound is sharp. Hales and collaborators later verified the whole argument in the formal Flyspeck project.

concepts.c:sphere-packing: The theorem bounds the density of every sphere packing.
concepts.c:lattice-discrete-subgroup: The face-centred cubic packing is a lattice packing that reaches the bound.
concepts.c:planar-graph: Possible counterexamples are encoded as a finite list of plane graphs.
concepts.c:linear-programming: Linear programs bound the score of each plane graph.

source.ref: T. C. Hales, A proof of the Kepler conjecture, Annals of Mathematics 162 (2005), 1065-1185
source.note: The steps follow the structure of Hales's proof; see also the formal proof by T. Hales and others, Forum of Mathematics, Pi 5 (2017), e2.

statement: Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional [Koszul algebra](c:koszul-algebra) over a field, with $A_0$ semisimple and finite-dimensional Koszul dual $A^!$. Then the bounded [derived categories](c:derived-category) of finitely generated graded modules are equivalent, $D^b(A\text{-gmod})\simeq D^b(A^!\text{-gmod})$, and the equivalence sends simple modules to shifted projective modules.

hypotheses.text: The algebra $A=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}A_i$ is a finite-dimensional [graded algebra](c:graded-algebra) over a field, $A_0$ is semisimple, and $A_1$ generates $A$ over $A_0$.
The algebra $A$ is [Koszul](c:koszul-algebra): the module $A_0$ has a linear projective resolution.
The Koszul dual, the opposite of the [Ext](c:ext-functor) algebra of $A_0$, is finite dimensional.

conclusion: There is an equivalence of triangulated categories $D^b(A\text{-gmod})\simeq D^b(A^!\text{-gmod})$ that sends each simple module to a shifted indecomposable projective module.

proofs.name: Koszul functor of Beilinson, Ginzburg and Soergel
proofs.slogan: Build the Koszul functor from the Koszul complex and show that the same construction for the dual algebra is its quasi-inverse.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of the cited proof, for finite-dimensional $A$ and $A^!$, where both bounded derived categories are defined; the general case needs partially bounded derived categories.

roles.why: The grading and the semisimple $A_0$ define the Ext algebra and the functor with its degree bookkeeping.
Koszulity makes the Koszul complex a linear resolution and makes the two composites the identity.
Finite dimension of $A^!$ makes the dual construction preserve bounded derived categories.

steps.slogan: Define the Koszul dual as the Ext algebra of the degree-zero part.
steps.detail: The Yoneda [Ext](c:ext-functor) algebra $\operatorname{Ext}_A^\bullet(A_0,A_0)$ is graded by cohomological and internal degree. For a Koszul algebra it is the [quadratic](c:quadratic-algebra) dual $A^!$, generated by $A_1^*$ with the orthogonal relations, and $A^!$ is again Koszul with $(A^!)^!=A$.

steps.slogan: Resolve $A_0$ by the linear Koszul complex.
steps.detail: Koszulity makes $\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(A_0,A_0\langle j\rangle)$ vanish unless $i=j$. So the minimal resolution of $A_0$ is the [Koszul complex](c:koszul-complex), with term $A\otimes_{A_0}(A^!_i)^*$ in degree $i$.

steps.slogan: Build the Koszul functor from complexes of graded $A$-modules to complexes of graded $A^!$-modules.
steps.detail: Start from $A^!\otimes_{A_0}M$ and add a Koszul differential given by the canonical element of $A^!_1\otimes A_1$. Match the gradings and shifts so that the result is a complex of graded $A^!$-modules.

steps.slogan: Show that the functor is an equivalence by building its quasi-inverse from the dual algebra.
steps.detail: The same construction for $A^!$ gives a functor in the other direction. The two composites are quasi-isomorphic to the identities because the Koszul complexes of $A$ and of $A^!$ are exact (step 2). Finite dimension of $A$ and $A^!$ makes both functors preserve bounded derived categories.

steps.slogan: Compute that simple modules go to shifted projective modules.
steps.detail: The Koszul complex resolves the simple module $L$ by free modules (step 2), so the image of $L$ under the equivalence is an indecomposable projective $A^!$-module, with a shift of internal and cohomological degree. The equivalence thus exchanges simple modules and shifted projectives.

concepts.c:koszul-algebra: Koszulity is the hypothesis that makes the duality work.
concepts.c:graded-algebra: The grading organizes the Ext algebra and the functor.
concepts.c:derived-category: The equivalence is an equivalence of bounded derived categories.
concepts.c:ext-functor: The Ext algebra of $A_0$ defines the Koszul dual.
concepts.c:quadratic-algebra: The Koszul dual of a Koszul algebra is its quadratic dual.
concepts.c:koszul-complex: The Koszul complex is the linear resolution that builds the functor.

source.ref: A. Beilinson, V. Ginzburg and W. Soergel, Koszul duality patterns in representation theory, Journal of the American Mathematical Society 9 (1996), 473-527
source.note: The steps follow Chapter 2 of the paper: the Ext algebra, the Koszul complex, the Koszul functor and its quasi-inverse.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite connected [planar graph](c:planar-graph) embedded in the plane, with dual graph $G^*$, and let $K,K^*>0$ satisfy $\sinh2K\,\sinh2K^*=1$. Then the [Ising](c:ising-model) [partition functions](c:partition-function) satisfy $Z_G(K)=2^{|V|-1}(\cosh K)^{|E|}e^{-K^*|E|}Z_{G^*}(K^*)$.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is a finite connected plane multigraph, so [planar](c:planar-graph), with dual graph $G^*$.

The function $Z_G(K)=\sum_{\sigma\in\{\pm1\}^V}\exp\bigl(K\sum_{ij\in E}\sigma_i\sigma_j\bigr)$ is the [partition function](c:partition-function) of the Ising model on $G$ without a field, and $Z_{G^*}$ is the same sum on $G^*$.
The couplings $K,K^*>0$ satisfy $\sinh2K\,\sinh2K^*=1$.

conclusion: $Z_G(K)=2^{|V|-1}(\cosh K)^{|E|}e^{-K^*|E|}Z_{G^*}(K^*)$, where $V$ and $E$ are the vertex and edge sets of $G$.

proofs.name: High- and low-temperature expansions
proofs.slogan: Expand $Z_G$ over even subgraphs, expand $Z_{G^*}$ over domain walls, and match the two sums through planar duality.
proofs.scope: The identity is exact for every finite connected plane multigraph, with loops and multiple edges allowed. It is the finite form of the Kramers-Wannier duality of the Ising model.

roles.why: Planarity makes cuts of $G^*$ correspond to even subgraphs of $G$, and $G^*$ is connected.
The Ising weights are expanded at high temperature on $G$ and at low temperature on $G^*$.
The relation between $K$ and $K^*$ makes the two expansions have the same weights.

steps.slogan: Expand the partition function in even subgraphs at high temperature.
steps.detail: Write $e^{K\sigma_i\sigma_j}=\cosh K\,(1+t\sigma_i\sigma_j)$ with $t=\tanh K$. Expand the product over edges and sum over spins: a term survives only if every vertex has even degree in the chosen edge set $A$, and it contributes $2^{|V|}$. So $Z_G(K)=2^{|V|}(\cosh K)^{|E|}\sum_{A\text{ even}}t^{|A|}$.

steps.slogan: Expand the dual partition function in domain walls at low temperature.
steps.detail: On the connected graph $G^*$ the edges with unequal end spins form a cut, and each cut comes from exactly two spin configurations. Since $e^{K^*\sigma\sigma'}=e^{K^*}e^{-2K^*[\sigma\ne\sigma']}$, $Z_{G^*}(K^*)=2e^{K^*|E|}\sum_{D\text{ cut}}e^{-2K^*|D|}$.

steps.slogan: Match the cuts of the dual graph with the even subgraphs of $G$.
steps.detail: For a connected plane graph the cycles of $G$ correspond to the minimal cuts of $G^*$ through the dual edges (Diestel, Graph Theory, Section 4.6). The map $A\mapsto A^*$ on edge sets is linear over $\mathbb F_2$, even subgraphs are sums of cycles, and cuts are sums of minimal cuts. So it maps the even subgraphs of $G$ bijectively onto the cuts of $G^*$, with $|A^*|=|A|$.

steps.slogan: Choose the dual coupling so that the two sums have the same weights.
steps.detail: Put $t=\tanh K$. Since $\sinh2K=2t/(1-t^2)$, the relation $\sinh2K\sinh2K^*=1$ holds exactly when $e^{-2K^*}=t$, because then $\sinh2K^*=(1-t^2)/(2t)$. Then $t^{|A|}=e^{-2K^*|A^*|}$, so by step 3 the sums of steps 1 and 2 are one sum $S$.

steps.slogan: Eliminate the common sum to get the duality of the partition functions.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 give $Z_G(K)=2^{|V|}(\cosh K)^{|E|}S$ and $Z_{G^*}(K^*)=2e^{K^*|E|}S$. Dividing the first by the second gives $Z_G(K)=2^{|V|-1}(\cosh K)^{|E|}e^{-K^*|E|}Z_{G^*}(K^*)$, because $G$ and $G^*$ have the same number of edges.

concepts.c:planar-graph: Planar duality turns domain walls of $G^*$ into even subgraphs of $G$.
concepts.c:ising-model: The Ising model defines the weights that the expansions use.
concepts.c:partition-function: The theorem is an identity between two partition functions.

source.note: The argument of Kramers and Wannier, Statistics of the two-dimensional ferromagnet, Part I, Physical Review 60 (1941), 252-262, in the combinatorial form for plane graphs; the correspondence of cycles and cuts is in Diestel, Graph Theory, Section 4.6.

statement: Let $X$ be a complete separable [computable metric space](c:computable-metric-space) and $Y$ a computable metric space. If $f$ is [computable](c:computable-function) on the computable points of $X$, then $f$ is effectively continuous: from an index of a computable point $x$ and a number $k$ one computes $n$ such that $d(f(x),f(y))<2^{-k}$ for every computable point $y$ with $d(x,y)<2^{-n}$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a complete separable [computable metric space](c:computable-metric-space).
The space $Y$ is a computable metric space.

A partial [computable function](c:computable-function) maps every index of a computable point $x$ of $X$ to an index of the point $f(x)$, and it maps indices of equal points to indices of equal points.

conclusion: An algorithm turns an index of a computable point $x$ and a number $k$ into $n$ such that every computable $y$ with $d(x,y)<2^{-n}$ has $d(f(x),f(y))<2^{-k}$.

proofs.name: Self-referential point by the recursion theorem
proofs.slogan: Assume that continuity fails, build with the recursion theorem a computable point on which the algorithm for $f$ contradicts itself, and read the modulus off the uniform construction.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of the Kreisel-Lacombe-Shoenfield-Ceitin argument. The recursion-theorem construction of step 3 is the delicate part; it is described here, not carried out.

roles.why: Completeness and separability give names of points by fast Cauchy sequences of computable dense points.
The computable metric on $Y$ lets the algorithm's answer be compared with $f(x)$ at a fixed precision.
The algorithm for $f$ runs on the index of the constructed point, and extensionality fixes its answer.

steps.slogan: Name computable points by indices of fast Cauchy sequences.
steps.detail: In the [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space) $X$ a computable point is the limit of a computable [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) of points from the dense computable sequence, with $d(x_m,x_{m+1})<2^{-m}$. A program that computes the sequence is an index of the point. The algorithm for $f$ acts on such indices and respects equality of points.

steps.slogan: Assume that no precision $n$ works at a computable point $x$.
steps.detail: Fix a computable point $x$ and a precision $k$, and suppose that no $n$ works. Then for every $n$ some computable point $y$ has $d(x,y)<2^{-n}$ and $d(f(x),f(y))\ge2^{-k}$.

steps.slogan: Build a computable point from its own index by the recursion theorem.
steps.detail: Build a computable point $z$ whose program knows its own index and runs the algorithm for $f$ on that index until it outputs an approximation $q$ of $f(z)$ with error below $2^{-k-2}$. Until then $z$ copies $x$. When $q$ appears, $z$ stays on $x$ if $q$ is more than $2^{-k-1}$ from $f(x)$, and otherwise switches to a bad point $y$ near $x$. The switch is made effective and keeps $z$ a fast Cauchy sequence.

steps.slogan: Compare the answer of the algorithm on $z$ with extensionality to refute the assumption.
steps.detail: If the run never halts, $z$ equals $x$ as a point, so extensionality forces an answer on the index of $z$. If it halts and $z$ stays on $x$, then $q$ is far from $f(z)=f(x)$. If it halts and $z$ switches, then $q$ is near $f(x)$ but far from $f(z)=f(y)$. Every case contradicts the error bound on $q$, so a suitable $n$ exists.

steps.slogan: Make the argument uniform to compute the modulus.
steps.detail: The construction depends only on the index of $x$, the algorithm for $f$ and the number $k$. An algorithm that searches the construction for the stage of the halting run therefore computes $n$ from an index of $x$ and $k$.

concepts.c:computable-metric-space: The theorem is about functions between computable metric spaces.
concepts.c:computable-function: Computability of $f$ gives the algorithm that runs on the constructed point.
concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness lets fast Cauchy sequences name the points of $X$.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: Computable fast Cauchy sequences are the names of computable points.

source.ref: G. S. Ceitin, Algorithmic operators in constructive metric spaces, Trudy Matematicheskogo Instituta imeni V. A. Steklova 67 (1962), 295-361; English translation in American Mathematical Society Translations, Series 2, 64 (1967), 1-80
source.note: The case of the Baire space is due to Kreisel, Lacombe and Shoenfield, Partial recursive functionals and effective operations, in Constructivity in Mathematics (A. Heyting, ed.), North-Holland, 1959, pp. 290-297; Ceitin extends it to constructive metric spaces.

statement: Let $M$ be a [module](c:module) of finite length, that is, with the ascending and descending [chain conditions](c:chain-condition) on submodules. Then $M$ is a finite [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of [indecomposable modules](c:indecomposable-module). If $M\cong M_1\oplus\dots\oplus M_n\cong N_1\oplus\dots\oplus N_m$ with all $M_i,N_j$ indecomposable, then $m=n$ and $M_i\cong N_{\pi(i)}$ for a permutation $\pi$.

hypotheses.text: The object $M$ is a [module](c:module) over a ring $R$.
The module $M$ satisfies the ascending and descending [chain conditions](c:chain-condition) on submodules, so it has finite length.

conclusion: The module $M$ is a finite direct sum of indecomposable modules, and the summands are unique up to isomorphism and order.

proofs.name: Fitting lemma and local endomorphism rings
proofs.slogan: Decompose by induction on length, show that the endomorphism ring of an indecomposable is local, and exchange one summand at a time.
proofs.scope: The module form of the theorem. The group form, with chain conditions on normal subgroups, follows the same exchange scheme with normal endomorphisms and is not written out here.

roles.why: The decomposition and the endomorphism rings live in the category of $R$-modules.
Finite length gives the induction on length, Fitting's lemma, and the fact that injective endomorphisms are automorphisms.

steps.slogan: Split the module into indecomposables by induction on its length.
steps.detail: If $M=0$ it is the empty sum. If $M\ne0$ is not [indecomposable](c:indecomposable-module), then $M=A\oplus B$ with $A,B\ne0$ of smaller length, which exists because the length is finite. By induction both $A$ and $B$ are finite direct sums of indecomposables, and so is $M$.

steps.slogan: Show that an endomorphism of an indecomposable module is nilpotent or an automorphism.
steps.detail: Let $f\in\operatorname{End}(M)$ with $M$ of length $\ell$. The chains $\ker f^j$ and $\operatorname{im}f^j$ become constant for $j\ge\ell$, which gives Fitting's decomposition $M=\ker f^\ell\oplus\operatorname{im}f^\ell$. If $M$ is indecomposable, either $\operatorname{im}f^\ell=0$ and $f$ is nilpotent, or $\ker f^\ell=0$ and $f$ is an automorphism.

steps.slogan: Show that the endomorphism ring of an indecomposable module is local.
steps.detail: Let $f,g$ be non-automorphisms with $f+g=u$ an automorphism. Then $u^{-1}f$ and $u^{-1}g$ are nilpotent by step 2 and add up to $1$, which is impossible because $1-a$ is invertible for nilpotent $a$. A product with a non-automorphism is a non-automorphism, since an injective endomorphism of finite length is onto. So the non-units form an ideal and the [endomorphism ring](c:endomorphism-ring) is a [local ring](c:local-ring).

steps.slogan: Match one summand of the first decomposition with one summand of the second.
steps.detail: Let $\iota_i,\pi_i$ and $\iota'_j,\pi'_j$ be the inclusions and projections of the two decompositions. Then $1_{M_1}=\sum_j\alpha_j\beta_j$ with $\beta_j=\pi'_j\iota_1\colon M_1\to N_j$ and $\alpha_j=\pi_1\iota'_j\colon N_j\to M_1$. The non-units of the local ring $\operatorname{End}(M_1)$ are closed under addition, so some $\alpha_j\beta_j$ is a unit; renumber so that $j=1$. Then $\beta_1$ is a split monomorphism, and $N_1$ indecomposable makes it an isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Replace the summand $M_1$ by $N_1$ inside $M$.
steps.detail: Define $\theta\colon M\to M$ as $\iota'_1\beta_1$ on $M_1$ and the identity on $M_2\oplus\dots\oplus M_n$. If $\theta(m_1+m')=0$, applying $\pi_1$ gives $\alpha_1\beta_1m_1=0$, so $m_1=0$ and then $m'=0$. An injective endomorphism of a module of finite length is an automorphism, so $M=\theta(M)=N_1\oplus M_2\oplus\dots\oplus M_n$.

steps.slogan: Cancel the matched summand, apply induction, and combine with existence.
steps.detail: From $M=N_1\oplus M_2\oplus\dots\oplus M_n=N_1\oplus N_2\oplus\dots\oplus N_m$ we get $M_2\oplus\dots\oplus M_n\cong M/N_1\cong N_2\oplus\dots\oplus N_m$. Induction on $n$ gives $n-1=m-1$ and a matching of the summands. Step 1 gives a decomposition, so the theorem follows.

concepts.c:module: The theorem decomposes a module over a ring.
concepts.c:chain-condition: Finite length gives induction on length and Fitting's lemma.
concepts.c:direct-sum: The theorem writes the module as a direct sum of pieces.
concepts.c:indecomposable-module: Indecomposable summands are the pieces that are unique.
concepts.c:endomorphism-ring: The ring of endomorphisms of a summand controls the exchange.
concepts.c:local-ring: Locality makes some term of the sum a unit.

source.note: The classical proof by Fitting's lemma and local endomorphism rings, as in M. F. Atiyah, On the Krull-Schmidt theorem with application to sheaves, Bulletin de la Societe Mathematique de France 84 (1956), 307-317.

statement: In a finite [extensive-form game](c:extensive-form-game), if player $i$ has [perfect recall](c:perfect-recall), then every [mixed strategy](c:mixed-strategy) of $i$ has a [behavior strategy](c:behavior-strategy) that gives every terminal node the same probability, whatever the other players do.

hypotheses.text: The game is a finite [extensive-form game](c:extensive-form-game): a finite tree, with chance moves allowed.
Player $i$ has [perfect recall](c:perfect-recall): all nodes of an information set share the same earlier information sets and actions of $i$.
The strategy $\sigma_i$ is a [mixed strategy](c:mixed-strategy): a probability distribution on the pure strategies of $i$.

conclusion: There is a [behavior strategy](c:behavior-strategy) $\beta_i$ of $i$ such that, against every pure strategy profile of the other players, $\beta_i$ and $\sigma_i$ give each terminal node the same probability.

proofs.name: Conditional probabilities of the mixed strategy
proofs.slogan: Define the behavior strategy by conditional probabilities of the mixed strategy and check by telescoping that every terminal node keeps its probability.
proofs.scope: The direction from mixed to behavior strategies. The converse, a mixed strategy equivalent to a given behavior strategy, holds without perfect recall by taking the product of the local distributions.

roles.why: A finite tree makes the path to each terminal node finite, so probabilities are finite products.
Perfect recall makes the set of strategies that reach an information set independent of the node.
The mixed strategy supplies the probabilities that the conditional distributions are built from.

steps.slogan: Write the probability of a terminal node as a product over the players.
steps.detail: For a terminal node $z$ let $c(z)$ be the product of the chance probabilities on the path to $z$, and let $S_j(z)$ be the set of pure strategies of player $j$ that choose the actions of $j$ on that path. For independent mixed strategies, $P(z)=c(z)\prod_j\sigma_j(S_j(z))$. So it suffices to match $\sigma_i(S_i(z))$ by a behavior strategy for every $z$.

steps.slogan: Use perfect recall to describe the pure strategies that reach an information set.
steps.detail: By perfect recall all nodes of an information set $I$ of $i$ share one history $(I_1,a_1),\dots,(I_r,a_r)$ of earlier information sets and actions of $i$. So the set $S_i(I)$ of pure strategies that can reach $I$ is $\{s:s(I_l)=a_l\text{ for }l\le r\}$, and it does not depend on the node. Along a path, $S_i(I_{k+1})=S_i(I_k)\cap\{s:s(I_k)=a_k\}$.

steps.slogan: Define the behavior strategy by conditional probabilities of the mixed strategy.
steps.detail: If $\sigma_i(S_i(I))>0$, put $\beta_i(I)(a)=\sigma_i(S_i(I)\cap\{s:s(I)=a\})/\sigma_i(S_i(I))$. Otherwise let $\beta_i(I)$ be any distribution on the actions at $I$. The sets $S_i(I)$ are well defined by step 2, so $\beta_i$ is a [behavior strategy](c:behavior-strategy).

steps.slogan: Telescope the conditional probabilities along the path to a terminal node.
steps.detail: Let $z$ have the moves $(I_1,a_1),\dots,(I_r,a_r)$ of $i$. By step 2, $\sigma_i(S_i(I_{k+1}))=\sigma_i(S_i(I_k)\cap\{s(I_k)=a_k\})$, so $\prod_k\beta_i(I_k)(a_k)$ telescopes to $\sigma_i(S_i(z))$ when all $\sigma_i(S_i(I_k))>0$. If some value is zero, the first zero is at a $k\ge2$, so $\beta_i(I_{k-1})(a_{k-1})=0$ and $\sigma_i(S_i(z))=0$ too.

steps.slogan: Compare the terminal-node probabilities of the two strategies.
steps.detail: In $P(z)=c(z)\prod_j\sigma_j(S_j(z))$ replace $\sigma_i$ by $\beta_i$. The factor of player $i$ becomes $\prod_k\beta_i(I_k)(a_k)=\sigma_i(S_i(z))$ by step 4, and all other factors stay the same. So every terminal node has the same probability against every pure strategy profile of the others.

statement: Assume the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice). If $\kappa_i<\lambda_i$ are [cardinal numbers](c:cardinal-number) for all $i\in I$, then $\sum_{i\in I}\kappa_i<\prod_{i\in I}\lambda_i$, where the sum is the size of the disjoint union and the product is the size of the Cartesian product.

hypotheses.text: The [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) holds.
For every $i\in I$ the [cardinal numbers](c:cardinal-number) satisfy $\kappa_i<\lambda_i$.

formal.difference: mathlib works in classical logic, so the axiom of choice needs no hypothesis. It states the inequality for functions $f,g$ from any index type to the cardinals, with the sum and the product given by sigma and pi types.

proofs.name: Diagonal argument
proofs.slogan: Assume an injection of the product into the sum, invert it, and build an element of the product that the inverse cannot reach.
proofs.scope: Any index set $I$, including $I=\emptyset$ where the sum is $0$ and the product is $1$. The axiom of choice is used to compare cardinals, to invert the injection and to choose the missed values.

roles.why: Choice makes cardinals comparable, gives the inverse of the injection, and picks the missed values.
The strict inequality $\kappa_i<\lambda_i$ makes each product factor nonempty and each slice map non-onto.

steps.slogan: Reduce the strict inequality to the absence of an injection from the product into the sum.
steps.detail: Choose sets $A_i,B_i$ with $|A_i|=\kappa_i$ and $|B_i|=\lambda_i$, so the sum is $|\bigsqcup A_i|$ and the product is $|\prod B_i|$. By the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) cardinals are linearly ordered, so it is enough to show that no injection $F\colon\prod B_i\to\bigsqcup A_i$ exists. Assume that such an $F$ exists.

steps.slogan: Turn the injection into a surjection from the sum onto the product.
steps.detail: Each $B_i$ is nonempty because $\lambda_i>\kappa_i$, so $\prod B_i$ is nonempty by choice. Hence $F$ has a left inverse $G\colon\bigsqcup A_i\to\prod B_i$ with $G\circ F=\mathrm{id}$, and $G$ is surjective.

steps.slogan: Pick in each coordinate a value that the $i$-th slice misses.
steps.detail: Fix $i$. The map $a\mapsto G(i,a)(i)$ from $A_i$ to $B_i$ is not onto, since otherwise $\lambda_i\le\kappa_i$. By choice pick $c_i\in B_i$ outside its image, for all $i$ at once.

steps.slogan: Form the diagonal element and derive a contradiction with surjectivity.
steps.detail: The tuple $c=(c_i)$ lies in $\prod B_i$. Since $G$ is surjective, $c=G(j,a)$ for some $(j,a)$, so $c_j=G(j,a)(j)$ lies in the image of the $j$-th slice map, against the choice of $c_j$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the strict inequality holds.
steps.detail: The contradiction shows that no injection from the product into the sum exists. Hence $\prod\lambda_i\not\le\sum\kappa_i$, and the linear order of the cardinals gives $\sum\kappa_i<\prod\lambda_i$.

concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: Choice compares cardinals, inverts the injection and picks the missed values.
concepts.c:cardinal-number: The theorem compares sizes of sets given as cardinal numbers.
concepts.c:cardinal-arithmetic: The sum and the product of cardinals are sizes of the disjoint union and the product.

source.note: mathlib assumes an injection of the product into the sum, takes a left inverse with Function.invFun, picks a missed value in each coordinate with choose, and reaches the diagonal contradiction.

statement: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be [independent](c:independence) [Bernoulli](c:bernoulli-distribution) variables with $P(X_i=1)=p_i$, $S_n=\sum_iX_i$ and $\lambda=\sum_ip_i$. Then $\sum_{k\ge0}\bigl|P(S_n=k)-e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!\bigr|\le2\sum_ip_i^2$, with strict inequality if some $p_i>0$. The left side is twice the [total variation distance](c:total-variation-distance) to the [Poisson distribution](c:poisson-distribution) with mean $\lambda$.

hypotheses.text: Each $X_i$ is a [Bernoulli](c:bernoulli-distribution) variable with $P(X_i=1)=p_i$ for some $p_i\in[0,1]$.
The variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are [independent](c:independence).

conclusion: The $\ell^1$ distance between the law of $S_n$ and the Poisson law with mean $\lambda$ is at most $2\sum_ip_i^2$, and it is strictly less if some $p_i>0$.

proofs.name: Coupling with Poisson variables
proofs.slogan: Couple each Bernoulli variable with a Poisson variable, add the independent pairs, and bound the chance that the sums differ.
proofs.scope: All $n\ge1$ and all $p_i\in[0,1]$. If every $p_i=0$ both sides are zero, which is why the strict inequality needs some $p_i>0$.

roles.why: Each Bernoulli law is coupled with a Poisson law of the same mean at cost $p_i(1-e^{-p_i})$.
Independence lets the coupled pairs be taken independent, so the sums have the right laws.

steps.slogan: Couple each Bernoulli variable with a Poisson variable of the same mean.
steps.detail: For $p\in[0,1]$ take $X\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ and $Y\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(p)$ on one space with $P(X=Y)=\sum_k\min(P(X=k),P(Y=k))$, a maximal coupling. Because $e^{-p}\ge1-p$, this sum is $(1-p)+pe^{-p}$, so $P(X\ne Y)=p(1-e^{-p})$.

steps.slogan: Take independent coupled pairs and add the coordinates.
steps.detail: Take independent pairs $(X_i,Y_i)$, coupled as in step 1 with $p=p_i$. Then $S=\sum X_i$ has the law of $S_n$, and $T=\sum Y_i$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda$, because a sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson with the summed mean.

steps.slogan: Bound the distance between the two laws by the probability that $S$ and $T$ differ.
steps.detail: Let $E=\{k:P(S=k)>P(T=k)\}$. Then $\sum_k|P(S=k)-P(T=k)|=2\,(P(S\in E)-P(T\in E))\le2P(S\ne T)$, because the events $\{S\in E\}$ and $\{T\in E\}$ can differ only inside $\{S\ne T\}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the probability of a difference by the union bound.
steps.detail:
The event $\{S
e T\}$ lies inside $ igcup_i\{X_i
e Y_i\}$. So $P(S
e T)\le\sum_iP(X_i
e Y_i)=\sum_ip_i(1-e^{-p_i})$.

steps.slogan: Estimate each term by $p_i^2$ and collect the bound.
steps.detail: Since $1-e^{-p}\le p$ with equality only at $p=0$, each term satisfies $p_i(1-e^{-p_i})\le p_i^2$, strictly when $p_i>0$. Steps 3 and 4 then give $\sum_k|P(S_n=k)-e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!|\le2\sum_ip_i^2$, strictly if some $p_i>0$.

concepts.c:independence: Independence lets the coupled pairs be independent and the sums add up.
concepts.c:bernoulli-distribution: Each summand is a Bernoulli variable coupled with a Poisson variable.
concepts.c:total-variation-distance: The left side is twice the total variation distance to the Poisson law.
concepts.c:poisson-distribution: The Poisson law is the approximating distribution that the coupling reaches.

source.note: The coupling proof of Hodges and Le Cam (1960); see J. M. Steele, Le Cam's inequality and Poisson approximations, American Mathematical Monthly 101 (1994), 48-54.
